title: From a measured surface to a usable asset

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A scanner measures a tiny surface, and the result is a grid of heights. What do you do with that grid?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's one thing, but the post is about going further. TrueMapData is Antoine's Python library for reading captures from TrueMap and GelSight. It exposes the heights as NumPy arrays and gives you tools for analysis and graphics export.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A header, spatial metadata, and the grid itself, stored as float32 samples. The metadata matters, because a game texture can stretch over any range, but a measured surface needs its sample spacing to keep its real physical scale.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So size stays attached to the data.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. And before exporting anything, he inspects the surface: a heatmap, a three-D view, profiles along a row or column, contours. Then you can derive a normal map for shading, a displacement map that carries height, or even a mesh in formats like STL, OBJ or glTF.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the scale still matters when you tile a texture on a mesh?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The apply-on-mesh path uses the template's bounds, the millimeters-per-pixel value and the capture's dimensions to set the tiling, so the scan's size connects to the surface receiving it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Roughness describes a surface at one moment, using ISO 25178 parameters through a separate package called Surfalize. Wear compares captures over time. Before subtracting heights, the frames must share the same grid and region, so the library aligns them first.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Reference height minus current height. A positive loss means the current surface is lower. To get a physical volume, you also need the pixel spacing in both directions, and registration errors or mixed units would change the answer.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the figures in the post are examples, not thesis data.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Correct, they come from the repository README. The full write-up has the diagrams and commands.
